d: A wildly enthusiastic speech or piece of writing
ety: From Latin dithyrambus, from Ancient Greek δῑθύραμβος (dīthúrambos). According to the American Heritage Dictionary, it is of non-Indo-European origin (Pre-Greek substrate, Illyrian/Phrygian), related to θρίαμβος (thríambos) and ἴαμβος (íambos). Brandenstein also compares Sanskrit अङ्ग (aṅga, “member”).
s: While those who drown a truth’s empiric part In dithyramb or dogma turn frenetic; — Than whom no writer could be less poetic He left this lesson for all verse, all art.

d: A window above a door that is usually hinged to a horizontal crosspiece over the door
ety: From fan + light (“window; source of illumination”).
s: Limpet was out, but with a deal of struggling he managed to screw himself through the fanlight, removing in that process the dust of many ages.

d: A powerful circular current of water (usually the result of conflicting tides)
ety: The word was originally the name of a giant whirlpool off Norway in the Arctic Ocean which was said to destroy all ships that came close to it, likely the actual tidal pool system of Moskstraumen in Lofoten. It is borrowed from early modern Dutch maelstrom (“whirlpool”) (obsolete) (modern Dutch maalstroom), from malen (“to whirl around; to grind”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to
s: He escaped at last, dizzy from the maelstrom of conflicting emotions that had caught and whirled him.

d: A full skirt with a gathered waistband
ety: Borrowed from German Dirndl, a diminutive of Dirne (“girl”) (Austria, Bavaria), from Middle High German dierne (“girl; servant”), from Old High German diorna, thiorna (“girl; servant”), from Proto-West Germanic *þewernā (“maiden, young girl; female servant, handmaid”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tekʷ- (“to flow; to run”).
s: For a change, Selina was not in slacks, but in a simple dirndl and sandals.

d: A set of confused and meaningless statements
ety: From ragman roll (“long list; catalogue”). Recorded since c1736.
s: If you are alluding to Dostoevski’s worst novels, then, indeed, I dislike intensely The Karamazov Brothers and the ghastly Crime and Punishment rigmarole.

d: A small and compactly built upright piano
ety: Borrowed from Italian spinetta.
s: The invention was to have a Satyr lodged in a little spinet, by which her majesty and the prince were to come

d: Change completely the nature or appearance of
ety: 17th century; origin uncertain, but possibly from transmigure, transmigrate. It is also possible that this word is a formation derived from maugre, hence it originally signified the "evil eye", but under the influence of the former etymologies shifted its meaning to its sense of "transformation". Another possibility is a humorous blending of transfigure and modify.
s: "Just set the dial to "Calvin", and I'll transmogrify back to a boy."

d: Stop the flow of a liquid
ety: From Middle English stanch, stanche [and other forms], a variant of Middle English staunchen, staunche (“to stop the flow of blood, diarrhoea, or other bodily fluids; to alleviate, ease; to appease, assuage, satisfy; to cure; to overcome; to put an end to; to repress, suppress; of a river or stream: to stop flowing; of waters, wind, or weather: to become calm, subside; to extinguish or put out (a
s: A small amount of cotton can be stuffed into the nose to stanch the flow of blood if necessary.

d: Physical discomfort (as mild sickness or depression)
ety: From French malaise (“ill ease”), from mal- (“bad, badly”) + aise (“ease”). Compare ill at ease.
s: Volkswagen’s travails are symbolic of the nation’s overall economic malaise and a political crisis that collapsed the government in December, paving the way for early elections Feb. 23.

d: The psychological state of being irritated or annoyed
ety: From bother + -ation (suffix indicating an action or process, or its result).
s: At home he read too many papers. He was better off without his daily dose of world botheration, sham happenings, without newspaper phrases.

d: Be appropriate or necessary
ety: From Middle English behoven, bihoven (“to be necessary, requisite; to be compelled or required (to do something)”), from Old English behōfian (“to need; to be necessary”), from Proto-Germanic *bihōfōną (“to benefit, behove, need”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“to grab, seize”). The word is cognate with Old Frisian bihōvia (“to need”), Middle Low German behôven (“to need”) and Old Sa
s: I never over Horeb heard / The blast of advent blow; / No fire-faced prophet brought me word / Which way behoved me go.

d: Patient endurance especially of pain or distress
ety: From Middle English sufferaunce, from Anglo-Norman suffraunce, from Late Latin sufferentia. By surface analysis, suffer + -ance.
s: When his talk trespasses beyond sufferance, I chastise him.

d: Marked by up-to-dateness in dress and manners
ety: From late 18th century raff (“persons among the lowest class in society”) + -ish, still retained in contemporary English with riffraff. From Old French raffer (“to wear away”), of Germanic origin. Compare German raffen. Compare rip (“to tear”), rap (“to snatch”).
s: The smokers' most raffish outsider, Comstock, appeared to do nothing but smoke; Chris had never seen him inside the building.

d: More than is needed, desired, or required
ety: From Latin superērogātōrius (“supererogatory”), from superērogātiō (“payment in addition”), from superērogō (“pay out over and above”), from super (“above”) + ērogō (“pay out, expend”); from ex (“out of, from”) + rogō (“ask; request”).
s: It is, for example, not clear whether “love thy enemy” is a precept or a supererogatory counsel.

d: Formal expression of respect
ety: From Middle English devoir, borrowed from Middle French devoir, from Old French deveir, from Latin dēbēre (“to owe; ought, must”).
s: I should have long ere this paid my devoirs to the inhabitants of Raymond Castle.

d: Consider carefully and deeply; reflect upon; turn over in one’s mind
ety: First attested in 1570; borrowed from Latin cōgitātus, perfect passive participle of cōgitō (“to think”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).
s: Think, ladies! Cogitate! Sharpen up the edges of your wit.

d: A club that is used as a weapon
ety: From Middle English kuggel, from Old English cyċġel (“a large stick, cudgel”), from Proto-West Germanic *kuggil, from Proto-Germanic *kuggilaz (“a knobbed instrument”), derivative of Proto-Germanic *kuggǭ (“cog, swelling”), from Proto-Indo-European *gewgʰ- (“swelling, bow”), from Proto-Indo-European *gew- (“to bow, bend, arch, curve”), equivalent to cog + -el (diminutive suffix). Cognate with Midd
s: The guard hefted his cudgel menacingly and looked at the inmates.

d: Incite to commit a crime or an evil deed
s: He suborned his butler to cover up the murder of his wife.

d: Detrimental to health
ety: From in- + salubrious.
s: But while the were a few pockets of the city centre that were desirable places in which to live, for the most part London's traditional areas were overcrowded and insalubrious.

d: Armor that protects the wearer’s whole body
ety: From Latin cataphractes (“suit of armour”), from Ancient Greek κατάφρακτος (katáphraktos, “suit of armour”), from κατα- (kata-, prefix indicating a great degree or intensity) + φρακτός (phraktós, “protected; fenced in”) (from φράσσω (phrássō, “to fortify, secure; to fence in”)) + -της (-tēs, suffix forming nouns indicating a state of being).
s: Carmine streaks stained their limbs, their tunics and cataphracts; but little of the blood was theirs. They did not move like people with injuries.

d: Someone who is the first to think of or make something
ety: From Middle English artificer, from Middle French artificier, from Latin artificiarius.
s: And Zillah, she also bare Tubal-cain, an instructer of every artificer in brass and iron: and the sister of Tubal-cain was Naamah.

d: Narcotic consisting of an alcohol solution of opium or any preparation in which opium is the main ingredient
ety: From New Latin, from lādanum (“a gum resin”), from Ancient Greek λᾱ́δανον (lā́danon). Originally the same word as ladanum, labdanum, compare French laudanum, Italian laudano, ladano. Perhaps influenced by Latin laudō (“to praise”). See ladanum. Used by Paracelsus to refer to ladanum gum, and to a compound recipe containing pearls, but apparently not to any preparation of opium; this modern sense w
s: Whipping and abuse are like laudanum; you have to double the dose as the sensibilities decline.

d: The intellectual conception of a thing as it is in itself, not as it is known through perception
ety: From German Noumenon, from Ancient Greek νοούμενον (nooúmenon, “thing that is known”), passive present participle of νοέω (noéō, “I know”).
s: That, we have seen, is what prevents the two truths from collapsing into an appearance/reality or phenomenon/noumenon distinction.

d: Produce a literary work
ety: Originally a variant of indict; from Middle English enditen, endyten, from Old French enditer, from Late Latin indictāre, from in- + dictare (“to declare”). Doublet of indict.
s: My heart is inditing a good matter.

d: A decorative musical accompaniment (often improvised) added above a basic melody
ety: From Anglo-Norman descaunt, from Medieval Latin discantus. Doublet of discant.
s: Upon that simplest of themes how magnificent a descant!

d: Something unspecified whose name is either forgotten or not known
ety: Ante 1553. From gobbin (“piece, portion, slice”), from Middle English goboun, from Anglo-Norman gobon. Compare with English gobony (“line of alternating squares”).
s: I had to memorise so much dialogue that never makes it into the movie so I always have a plethora of extra gubbins I can't remember.

d: Tending to find and call attention to faults
ety: From Middle English capcious, from Middle French captieux, or its source, Latin captiōsus, from captiō.
s: But Peter Petrovich did not accept this retort. On the contrary, he became all the more captious and irritable, as though he were just hitting his stride.

d: An East Indian sailor
ety: From Hindustani لشکر / लश्कर (laśkar), from Persian لشکر (laškar). Doublet of askari.
s: As for the voyage itself, his account of Mauritius, where the ship stopped, saw the appearance of Muslim lascars.

d: Temporary fortification like a detached bastion
ety: Unadapted borrowing from French lunette, diminutive of lune (“moon”).
s: Sticking out of a crescent-shaped sand ridge of a type known as a lunette were some human bones.

d: Position in which the dancer has one leg raised behind and arms outstretched in a conventional pose
ety: Borrowed from French arabesque, from Italian arabesco, from arabo (“Arab”). By surface analysis, Arab + -esque.
s: For a man who condemned worldly pleasures he ate with elegance. She loved to watch the arabesque of fingers and two forks.

d: A singer of folk songs
ety: From Old Occitan trobar (“to find”) via Old French troubadour. Piecewise doublet of trouveur.
s: “"Not a human, not yet a vampire," to paraphrase one of your contemporary musical troubadours.”

d: The character flaw or error of a tragic hero that leads to his downfall
ety: From Ancient Greek ἁμαρτία (hamartía, “tragic failure, sinful nature”), from the verb ἁμαρτάνω (hamartánō, “to miss the mark”).
s: Creon's main hamartia was his excessive pride.

d: A composition that imitates or misrepresents somebody’s style, usually in a humorous way
ety: From French lampon (“satire, mockery, ridicule”), built on French lampons (“let us drink — a popular refrain for scurrilous songs”), from lamper (“to quaff, to swig”). : Littré quotes a satirical song mocking King Jacques II Stuart, fleeing Dublin, in 1691, and returning to France under the escort of Lauzun: :: Prenez soin de ma couronne, J'aurai soin de ma personne ; ("Take care of my crown, I wi
s: To say truth, Ma'am, 'tis very vulgar to Print and as my little Productions are mostly Satires and Lampoons I find they circulate more by giving copies in confidence to the Friends of the Parties—

d: Preaching the gospel of Christ in the manner of the early church
ety: From Ancient Greek κήρυγμα (kḗrugma, “proclamation, preaching”), from κηρύσσω (kērússō, “I proclaim, preach”), from κῆρυξ (kêrux, “herald”).
s: Many who encounter Jung do so within the community of the spirit, and some look to the personal myth of C. G. Jung in MDR as a contemporary gospel that contains the kerygma of a new dispensation.

d: A person who is bound to the land and owned by the feudal lord
ety: From Anglo-Norman vilein, variant of vilain; from Medieval Latin villanus (“field hand”), from Latin villa (“country home”). Doublet of villain.
s: "Then you're not - " "Darling," I said, "do you really see me in the position of a seigneur, driving my serfs and villeins before me with a whip - even if the triffids haven't overrun me first?"

d: A provocative Spanish courtship dance in triple time; performed by a man and a woman playing castanets
ety: Borrowed from Spanish fandango, of uncertain origin. Possibly related to Portuguese fado, or of West African origin.
s: What’s that fandango you’re using?

d: Assign great social importance to
ety: From lion + -ize.
s: Flare-riding is one of the most exotic and exhilarating sports in existence, and those who can dare and afford to do it are amongst the most lionized men in the Galaxy.

d: Making a chance decision by using lots (straws or pebbles etc.) that are thrown or drawn
ety: From Latin sortītiō.
s: Demarchy — also called sortition — is a form of governance that selects the representatives of the people as a random sample from a pool of candidates.

d: Worry unnecessarily or excessively
ety: First attested in 1599. Origin uncertain, but likely borrowed from dialectal Norwegian nigla (“to be stingy, to busy oneself with trifles”), ultimately from Old Norse hnøggr (“stingy; miserly”), related to Old English hnēaw (“stingy; niggardly”). More at niggard.
s: I can see him now with his one eye closed as he came niggling along, and didn't he just give me a grandfather's blessing!

d: A sudden and unexpected change of fortune or reverse of circumstances (especially in a literary work)
ety: From Late Latin peripetia, and its source Ancient Greek περιπέτεια (peripéteia), from περιπίπτω (peripíptō, “to change suddenly”), from περί (perí, “round, around, about”) + the stem of πίπτω (píptō, “to fall”).
s: Once more I was a man in a myth, incapable of understanding it, but somehow aware that understanding it meant it must continue, however sinister its peripeteia.
